events.event_title: Clovis-era occupation at the Gault site (deep-time context)
events.event_description_neutral: The Gault site near Florence holds a well-dated Clovis component of about 13,600-13,000 calibrated years before present; a mean OSL age for the Clovis deposits is 12,900 +/- 700 years. Older OSL ages of about 16,000-20,000 years from the adjacent Buttermilk Creek complex are contested.
communities_affected: Ancestral Indigenous peoples of the Clovis era
events.human_intervention_description: None documented. Archaeological context for the depth of human presence.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: pre-Clovis ages of about 16,000-20,000 years

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Peer-reviewed dating: Rodrigues et al. (2016); Waters et al. on the age of Clovis and on Buttermilk Creek (2018).

unverified_claims.claim: Clovis occupation "about 11,200 years BP" (input Report 2)
unverified_claims.flag_reason: Mixes uncalibrated radiocarbon years with calendar years; ruled wrong in CR Appendix A

events.event_title: Indigenous presence in Central Texas before and during early contact
events.event_description_neutral: Multiple ancestral Indigenous communities lived in and moved through Central Texas across the pre-contact and contact eras. Spanish records later grouped many South Texas bands under the umbrella term "Coahuiltecan"; the Tonkawa, Lipan Apache and, from the 1700s, Comanche appear in the historical record for the region.
events.human_intervention_description: None before contact. Later Spanish record-keeping imposed ethnolinguistic categories on many distinct bands.
events.primary_location_name: Central Texas: Colorado River basin and the margin of the Edwards Plateau

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: The Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma narrates Central Texas as ancestral homeland.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma, tribal history (as cited in CR sec. 2)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: The Lipan Apache entered Texas from the plains about 1600, and by 1730 ranged from the upper Brazos through the upper Colorado to the Pecos.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: N. McGown Minor, "The Lipan Homeland of Many Houses," Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas (2009); tribal timeline

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: The Tonkawa were independent bands that united in Central Texas in the early 1700s; newer evidence suggests a move from the high plains as late as the 1600s.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: TSHA Handbook of Texas, "Tonkawa Indians" (as excerpted by the Austin History Center resource list)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: The Tonkawa occupied prairie from the Llano River to the Canadian River from at least the eleventh century.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, "Tonkawas"

events.conflict_summary: Accounts differ on whether the Tonkawa are long resident in Central Texas or moved south from the plains in the 1600s. "Coahuiltecan" is a colonial umbrella term, not one nation, and the claim that Coahuiltecans were "the original inhabitants of Austin" is ruled too categorical.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: Tonkawa origins and ethnogenesis

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Archaeology and later colonial records; tribal histories; scholars disagree on Tonkawa origins.

unverified_claims.claim: Tonkawa formed from survivors of Caddo, Karankawa, Coahuiltecan and Lipan groups (input Report 2)
unverified_claims.resolving_record: Specialist ethnohistory, e.g. work cited in TSHA "Tonkawa Indians"

events.event_title: El Camino Real de los Tejas crossings in the Austin area
events.event_description_neutral: Routes of El Camino Real de los Tejas crossed the region at river and creek fords, for example Onion Creek at McKinney Falls.
events.human_intervention_description: Spanish colonial route-making between the Rio Grande and East Texas.
events.primary_location_name: Onion Creek ford, McKinney Falls (example crossing)
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Named in CR sec. 3.1; route details not re-verified.

unverified_claims.claim: Indigenous trade routes became El Camino Real and modern roads (input Report 2)
unverified_claims.resolving_record: National Park Service, El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail studies

events.event_title: Three Spanish missions placed on the Colorado River near Barton Springs
events.event_description_neutral: Three East Texas missions (San Francisco de los Neches, Nuestra Senora de la Purisima Concepcion, San Jose de los Nazonis) were moved to the Colorado River near present Barton Springs and Zilker Park by July 1730. In 1731 they moved again to the San Antonio River, where they were refounded on 5 March 1731.
communities_affected: Franciscan missionaries of the College of Queretaro
Indigenous communities of the Colorado River valley (not named in the located record)
Indigenous communities attached to the three East Texas missions
events.human_intervention_description: Franciscan and viceregal decision to relocate the missions after Spain scaled back the East Texas presidio in 1729.
events.primary_location_name: Colorado River near Barton Springs / Zilker Park (general area only)
events.geographic_context_notes: First dated colonial act inside the present city. The site lies outside the 1839 grid and entered the city only with later annexation. Show with a "general area" halo, not a pin.

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Mission and viceregal records treat the move as an administrative relocation of three missions after the East Texas presidio was reduced in 1729, followed by refounding at San Antonio on 5 March 1731.
perspective_accounts.source_name: Spanish colonial records as summarized by the Texas State Historical Association
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, "Travis County" and "Nuestra Senora de la Purisima Concepcion de Acuna Mission"

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: A state historical marker at Barton Springs Pool commemorates the three missions as having stood in this vicinity.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Texas Historical Commission marker, Barton Springs Pool, text reproduced in the Historical Marker Database (hmdb.org)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: No remains have been found; historians place the missions in this general area from documents alone.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Michael Barnes, "Where are the Spanish missions on the Colorado River?", Austin American-Statesman, 29 Aug 2015

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Coahuiltecan-descendant communities name Barton Springs as one of four sacred springs. This is a narrative about the place, not an account of the 1730 missions.
perspective_accounts.source_name: Miakan-Garza Band / Indigenous Cultures Institute, as attributed in the consolidated report
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Attributed in Consolidated Final Report sec. 3.10; not independently verified

events.conflict_summary: The location and the reason for the 1731 move are not established. One input report named a single mission and blamed epidemics and Apache raids; the located record shows three missions and does not support that cause for these missions.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: reason for the 1731 move
exact site: documents only, no archaeology

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Spanish-period documentation summarized by TSHA; Texas Historical Commission marker at Barton Springs Pool; no physical remains have been found.
events.documentation_gaps: No Indigenous account of this episode was located. Records that could help: 1730-31 mission correspondence (Bexar Archives; College of Queretaro records); consultation with tribal historic preservation offices.

unverified_claims.claim: Only one mission, San Jose de los Nazonis, stood at Barton Springs (input Report 1)
The missions left because of "devastating epidemics and relentless raids by the Apache" (input Report 1)

adjudication_notes: Three missions, not one: Report 2 and the Audit correct; Report 1 wrong (CR Appendix A).

related_events.note: The marker commemorates the missions.

impact_by_community.note: Extends the mission frontier for one year.
No located Indigenous account; effect on local communities is undocumented.

searchable_keywords: Central Texas bands named in Spanish records

events.event_title: San Xavier missions on the San Gabriel River
events.event_description_neutral: Spanish missions operated on the San Gabriel River near present Rockdale, Milam County, from 1746 to 1755, serving Yojuane, Deadose, Mayeye and related groups.
events.human_intervention_description: Crown and Franciscan decision to found missions for Central Texas groups.
events.primary_location_name: San Gabriel River near present Rockdale, Milam County (generalized)
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA Handbook of Texas; Audit correction to 1746-1755 upheld.
adjudication_notes: Dates 1746-1755 (not 1756): Report 2 and the Audit correct.
searchable_keywords: Central Texas bands named in Spanish records

events.event_title: Mission San Saba destroyed
events.event_description_neutral: Mission San Saba, founded for the Lipan Apache, was destroyed in 1758. Secondary sources describe Comanche pressure on the Lipan around the mission.
events.human_intervention_description: Spanish decision to site a mission for the Lipan; attack by opposing groups.
events.primary_location_name: San Saba River near present Menard
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA; Texas Beyond History (Fort McKavett).

unverified_claims.claim: Tonkawa chief El Mocho helped plan the 1758 attack (input Report 2)
unverified_claims.flag_reason: Likely error: his documented leadership dates to the 1770s-1780s
unverified_claims.resolving_record: TSHA biography of El Mocho; Bexar Archives

events.event_title: Stephen F. Austin's colonization begins (the Old Three Hundred)
events.event_description_neutral: Under Mexican colonization law, Stephen F. Austin's colony brought Anglo-American settlers into Texas from 1821, with the first cohort arriving 1822-1825. Settlers brought enslaved African Americans with them.
events.human_intervention_description: Empresario land-grant system under Mexican colonization law.
events.primary_location_name: Austin's Colony (lower Brazos and Colorado rivers)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Tejanos stood on both sides of the slavery question.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Cynthia Orozco, essay for Mexic-Arte Museum (as cited in CR sec. 3.1)

events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA; enslaved-population figure for 1825 not verified.

unverified_claims.claim: 443 of 1,790 people in the colony were enslaved by 1825 (input Report 2)
unverified_claims.flag_reason: Not replicated; TSHA reports a total near 1,800
unverified_claims.resolving_record: 1825 census of Austin's Colony (Austin Papers, Briscoe Center)

events.event_title: Mexico restricts (1827) and abolishes (1829) slavery
events.event_description_neutral: Coahuila y Tejas restricted slavery in 1827 and Mexico abolished it nationally in 1829, while Anglo colonists in Texas continued to hold enslaved people.
events.human_intervention_description: State constitution and national decree limiting slavery.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Dates as given in CR sec. 3.1; tie each to the primary statute before publication.

events.event_title: Hornsby Bend settlement
events.event_description_neutral: Reuben Hornsby settled at the bend of the Colorado River east of the future town site in 1832, an early Anglo foothold in the area.
communities_affected: Indigenous nations of the Colorado River valley
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Named in CR sec. 3.1.

events.event_title: Fort Colorado (Coleman's Fort)
events.event_description_neutral: A Republic of Texas ranger post, Fort Colorado or Coleman's Fort, was established east of the future town site in 1836.
events.human_intervention_description: Republic decision to garrison the Colorado River frontier.
events.primary_location_name: East of present Austin near Walnut Creek (approximate)
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Named in CR sec. 3.1; site location approximate.

events.event_title: President Lamar's message urging removal of Indigenous nations
events.event_description_neutral: In December 1838 President Mirabeau B. Lamar's message to the Congress of the Republic of Texas urged the removal of Indigenous nations, in words recorded as "total extinction or total expulsion."
communities_affected: Indigenous nations within the Republic of Texas
events.human_intervention_description: Executive policy statement of the Republic of Texas.
events.primary_location_name: Republic of Texas (message delivered at Houston)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Characterizes Republic-era Indian policy as ethnic cleansing.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Gary Clayton Anderson, The Conquest of Texas: Ethnic Cleansing in the Promised Land, 1820-1875 (University of Oklahoma Press, 2005)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Framed removal as necessary for the security and expansion of the Republic.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Message of President Lamar to Congress, December 1838 (Texas State Library and Archives)

events.conflict_summary: The record of the policy is not disputed. Labels differ: modern scholars such as Gary Clayton Anderson use "ethnic cleansing"; the Republic framed the policy as security.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: how the policy should be characterized

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Lamar-era records and Texas State Library documentation, as confirmed by the Audit.

events.event_title: Waterloo settlement surveyed
events.event_description_neutral: Waterloo, a small settlement founded by Jacob Harrell on the north bank of the Colorado, was surveyed by Edward Burleson in 1838. It became the site of Austin.
communities_affected: Indigenous nations using the river valley
events.primary_location_name: North bank of the Colorado at the future Congress Avenue
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA.

events.event_title: Enslaved workers build the first capital buildings
events.event_description_neutral: Edwin Waller hired enslaved labour to build the earliest government buildings and infrastructure of the new capital.
events.human_intervention_description: Hiring of enslaved workers for public construction.

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Enslaved people helped build the earliest city buildings and infrastructure; Waller hired enslaved labour.
perspective_accounts.source_name: Austin History Center, "You Are Here" project
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Austin History Center / City of Austin, "African Americans in Austin" (youarehereatx.org)

events.documentation_validity_evidence: City of Austin and the Austin History Center "You Are Here" project; individual lives are thinly recorded.

unverified_claims.claim: Early Austin was "entirely dependent" on enslaved labour (input Report 1)
unverified_claims.flag_reason: Counterfactual claim not shown by a population count

events.event_title: Austin founded as capital of the Republic of Texas
events.event_description_neutral: The Congress of the Republic chose the site in January 1839. Edwin Waller laid out a 640-acre, 14-block grid; the first lots sold on 1 August; President Lamar and cabinet arrived on 17 October; the city was incorporated on 27 December 1839.
communities_affected: Enslaved African Americans who built the town
Comanche, Tonkawa and Lipan Apache, whose ranges included the site
events.human_intervention_description: Deliberate siting of a national capital on the settlement frontier, and platting of a grid.
events.primary_location_name: Waller grid between Shoal and Waller creeks
events.geographic_context_notes: Defines "Austin" for the first time: one square mile. Every later boundary epoch is measured against this grid.

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Lamar's supporters framed the capital as the seat of a future empire.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: As summarized in CR sec. 3.2 from TSHA

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Houston-area critics called the site a dangerous frontier outpost.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: As summarized in CR sec. 3.2 from TSHA

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: In 1839 Austin lay on the fringe of the Penateka Comanche range.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Texas Beyond History, Fort McKavett exhibit, "Collisions"

events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA; City of Austin.

unverified_claims.claim: The grid "deliberately ignored Indigenous pathways" (input Report 1)
unverified_claims.flag_reason: States intent that no primary evidence supports; describe as effect

events.event_title: Council House killings in San Antonio
events.event_description_neutral: On 19 March 1840, during talks in San Antonio, Texas troops killed about thirty Penateka Comanche leaders and warriors and about five women and children after officials tried to hold the delegation.
communities_affected: Republic of Texas officials and troops
events.human_intervention_description: Republic policy demanding the return of all captives and the decision to detain a peace delegation.
events.primary_location_name: Council House, Main Plaza, San Antonio

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Records the deaths of thirty Penateka leaders and warriors and some five women and children at the hands of Texas troops.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Jodye Lynn Dickson Schilz, "Council House Fight," Handbook of Texas (TSHA)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Describes government troops massacring thirty-five Comanche men, women and children during peace talks.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Humanities Texas, "Texas Originals: Buffalo Hump"

events.conflict_summary: Texian accounts name it the Council House Fight; accounts from the Comanche side and some institutions call it a massacre of a peace delegation.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: framing: "fight" or "massacre"

events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA Handbook of Texas (Schilz).

related_events.note: Sources describe the raid as retaliation.

events.event_title: Great Raid and Battle of Plum Creek
events.event_description_neutral: In August 1840 Penateka war leader Buffalo Hump led a raid to the coast, striking Victoria and Linnville. Texas forces met the returning party at Plum Creek near present Lockhart.
events.human_intervention_description: Retaliation for the Council House killings; Republic military response.
events.primary_location_name: Plum Creek near Lockhart, Caldwell County
events.geographic_context_notes: Plum Creek lies inside the present five-county metro area.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA; Humanities Texas.

related_events.note: Sources describe the raid as retaliation.

events.event_title: Comanche boundary proposal refused by the Texas Senate
events.event_description_neutral: In 1844 Buffalo Hump met President Sam Houston. The Comanche and their allies agreed to stop raiding if Texans stayed off the Edwards Plateau; the Texas Senate refused to recognize the boundary.
events.human_intervention_description: Treaty negotiation and legislative refusal to recognize a territorial line.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: One institutional source retrieved; treaty text not consulted.
events.context_source_ref: NEW: Humanities Texas, "Texas Originals: Buffalo Hump" (https://www.humanitiestexas.org/node/7397)

events.event_title: Round Rock settled; moved to the railroad in 1876
events.event_description_neutral: Settled in 1848 as Brushy Creek and renamed Round Rock in 1854, the town moved to the new railroad line in 1876.
communities_affected: Tonkawa, whose camps lay along Brushy Creek
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA.

events.event_title: 1850 census: 791 enslaved people in Travis County
events.event_description_neutral: The 1850 census counted 791 enslaved people in Travis County.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA, "Travis County"; U.S. Census 1850.

events.event_title: Settlers petition for removal of the Tonkawa
events.event_description_neutral: In 1854 citizens of Williamson and other counties petitioned authorities to remove the Tonkawa, whose numbers had been cut by smallpox and war.
communities_affected: Anglo settlers of Williamson and nearby counties
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Single journalistic source; petition text not retrieved.
events.context_source_ref: NEW: Texas Highways, "Recognizing Local History: Tonkawa Tribe, the Original Texans" (https://texashighways.com/culture/recoginzing-local-history-tonkawa-tribe-the-original-texans/)

events.event_title: Tonkawa removed from Texas to Indian Territory
events.event_description_neutral: After placement on a Brazos River reservation in the mid-1850s (sources give 1855 or 1856), the Tonkawa were removed to Indian Territory in 1859.
events.human_intervention_description: Closure of the Texas reservations and removal north of the Red River.
events.primary_location_name: Brazos reservation to Indian Territory (Washita River)
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA; Encyclopedia of the Great Plains.

events.event_title: 1860 census: enslaved people are 39 percent of Travis County and 29 percent of Austin
events.event_description_neutral: Travis County: 3,136 enslaved people among 8,080 residents (38.8 percent). City of Austin: 1,019 enslaved among 3,546 residents (28.74 percent). About 35 percent of Austin family heads held enslaved people.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA ("Travis County"; "Austin, TX"); U.S. Census 1860. Geographic unit must be shown with each figure.

unverified_claims.flag_reason: No source located; omitted from the timeline
unverified_claims.resolving_record: 1860 U.S. Census slave schedules, Travis County

events.event_title: Attack on the Tonkawa in Indian Territory (called the Tonkawa Massacre)
events.event_description_neutral: On 23-24 October 1862 a coalition of other Native nations attacked the Tonkawa near the Wichita Agency, killing roughly 137-150 of about 300 people. Survivors returned to Texas and sheltered at Fort Griffin.
communities_affected: Delaware, Shawnee, Caddo and other nations named in sources
events.human_intervention_description: Civil War alignments in Indian Territory; older inter-tribal enmities.
events.conflict_summary: Some accounts stress Tonkawa alignment with Texas and the Confederacy and service as scouts; others stress older enmities.

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: cause of the attack

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Oklahoma Historical Society; TSHA; Encyclopedia of the Great Plains.

events.event_title: Freedom colonies founded in and around Austin
events.event_description_neutral: After emancipation, formerly enslaved people founded land-owning settlements in and around Austin. Michelle Mears documents at least fifteen, which she describes as disappearing by 1928.
communities_affected: Formerly enslaved African Americans and their descendants
events.human_intervention_description: Community land purchase and institution-building after emancipation.
events.primary_location_name: Austin and nearby rural Travis County

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: At least fifteen freedmen communities formed in Austin and nearby after emancipation and had disappeared by 1928.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Michelle M. Mears, And Grace Will Lead Me Home: African American Freedmen Communities of Austin, Texas, 1865-1928 (Texas Tech University Press, 2009)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Places these settlements within a statewide atlas of freedom colonies.
perspective_accounts.source_name: Andrea Roberts, Texas Freedom Colonies Project
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Texas Freedom Colonies Project, Atlas (thetexasfreedomcoloniesproject.com)

events.conflict_summary: Counts differ: at least fifteen (Mears), at least sixteen (input Report 1), more than a dozen (input Report 2).

documentation_validity_secondary.applies_to: number of colonies

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Mears (2009); Texas Freedom Colonies Project. Counts depend on the geographic definition.

events.primary_location_name: Wheatville (24th-26th St, Shoal Creek-Rio Grande St)
events.documentation_validity_evidence: Austin American-Statesman (Michael Barnes); Neill-Cochran House Museum.

events.event_title: Clarksville founded
events.event_description_neutral: Charles Clark (formerly Charles Griffin) bought land west of the town in 1871, founding Clarksville.

events.human_intervention_description: State siting of its flagship university.
events.documentation_validity_evidence: TSHA.

events.event_title: Final removal of the Tonkawa from Texas
events.event_description_neutral: In October 1884 the remaining Tonkawa, about 92 people, left Fort Griffin and travelled by rail from Cisco, Texas. They wintered at the Sac and Fox Agency, went on by wagon in spring 1885, and reached Oakland in present Kay County, Oklahoma, on 30 June 1885.
communities_affected: United States Army and Indian Office
events.human_intervention_description: Federal decision to remove the last Tonkawa community from Texas to Indian Territory.
events.primary_location_name: Fort Griffin, Texas, to Oakland, Indian Territory
events.geographic_context_notes: Happens outside the metro area, but closes the Central Texas story of a nation whose homeland accounts include the Austin area. On a metro-scale map show an off-map arrow with the route inset.

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: The Tonkawa Tribe narrates the journey as its Trail of Tears: by rail from Cisco in October 1884, a winter at the Sac and Fox Agency, wagons in spring, arrival at Oakland on 30 June 1885.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma, tribal history (tonkawatribe.com)

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Records the removal of the Tonkawa to the Oakland Agency in 1884-85 and the tribe's earlier presence in present Oklahoma in 1601.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, "Tonkawa"

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Settlers of Williamson and other counties had petitioned as early as 1854 for the Tonkawa to be removed.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Texas Highways, "Recognizing Local History: Tonkawa Tribe, the Original Texans"

perspective_accounts.perspective_text: Summarizes the Tonkawa as living in Central Texas and the southern plains until removal to a reservation in Indian Territory in 1884.
perspective_accounts.source_citation: Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, "Tonkawas"

events.documentation_validity_evidence: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma tribal history; Oklahoma Historical Society; Texas Highways.
